hello.note: Literally "I see you", used all day. The reply is Yebo, sawubona. To more than one person, Sanibonani (sah-nee-boh-NAH-nee)

how-are-you.note: To more than one person, or to show respect to an older person, Ninjani? (neen-JAH-nee)

im-well.note: Then ask back: Wena unjani? (WEH-nah oon-JAH-nee), and you?

good-morning.note: Zulu has no separate good morning: sawubona works all day. Friends may ask Uvuke kanjani? (oo-VOO-keh gahn-JAH-nee), how did you wake?

goodbye.note: "Stay well", said by the one leaving. The one staying says Hamba kahle (HAHM-bah GAH-shleh), go well

please.note: Literally "I ask", and it starts a request. The c is a click: see the guide

thank-you.note: Ngiyabonga kakhulu (gah-KOO-loo) means thank you very much

youre-welcome.note: Literally "it's fine". Welcome, to a guest, is Wamukelekile

yes.note: Also the cheerful answer to sawubona

no.note: A click, like a disapproving tsk, then ah. Cha, ngiyabonga is no, thank you

excuse-me.note: Sorry, and excuse me. The x is the click used to gee up a horse

my-name.note: ngu joins the front of the name. The audio uses Peter as the example name

where-from.note: Answer Ngivela e... (ngee-VEH-lah eh), I come from...

its-beautiful.note: Kakhulu (gah-KOO-loo) means very, and goes after the word

dont-understand.note: The q is a loud pop: see the guide

speak-slowly.note: Literally "I ask that you speak a little", the usual way to say slowly

repeat.note: Literally "I ask that you do it again"

speak-english.note: Most South Africans speak some English, but they warm to anyone who greets them in Zulu first

one.note: For prices, times, and phone numbers, most people use English numbers. Zulu ones are used for counting things

six.note: Literally "the thumb": counting on the fingers, the thumb is the sixth

eight.note: Literally "leave out two": ten fingers less two

thousand.note: Prices are in rand (R), and usually said in English

hundred-thousand.note: Literally "a hundred thousands". In practice, people say it in English

how-much.note: Literally "what money is it?" Point at the thing

would-like.note: Literally "I ask for...", the polite way to order anything. The audio uses ikhofi (ee-KOH-fee), a coffee, as the example

i-want.note: More direct than ngicela. The audio uses lokhu (LOH-koo), this one, as the example

do-you-have.note: Literally "is there...?", the easy way to ask in a shop. The audio uses amanzi (ah-MAHN-zee), water, as the example

discount.note: Literally "can you lower the price?" Bargaining is fine at craft markets and roadside stalls, not in shops

card.note: Cards are taken almost everywhere in South Africa, even at many market stalls

breakfast.note: Literally "is breakfast put in?" Ibhulakufesi comes from English

wifi.note: Zulu borrows freely from English for anything modern

toilet.note: Iphi? (EE-pee) means where is? Many people say the toilet in English, or the loo

taxi.note: In South Africa a taxi usually means a shared minibus taxi. For a private car, use a ride app or ask for a metered cab

left.note: The x is a click from the side of the tongue, like urging on a horse

train.note: From English steamer. The Gautrain links Johannesburg airport, Johannesburg, and Pretoria

airport.note: Literally "the landing place of the aeroplanes". Many just say i-airport

bus-station.note: Long-distance coaches like Intercape and Greyhound leave from the main stations

which-train.note: e joins the front of the place and means to. The audio uses eThekwini (eh-TEH-kwee-nee), Durban, as the example

two-tickets.note: The audio uses Durban as the example

trip-length.note: Literally "how much time does it take to go to...?" The audio uses Durban

delicious.note: Kumnandi means it's nice or tasty, and is used for anything enjoyable

allergic.note: Literally "I can't eat...", the clearest way to say it. Add the food: inhlanzi (een-SHLAHN-zee) fish, amantongomane (ah-mahn-tohn-goh-MAH-neh) peanuts, amaqanda (ah-mah-[q]AHN-dah) eggs. The audio uses peanuts

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.note: Literally "a table of two people, please"

beer.note: Traditional sorghum beer, shared at gatherings, is umqombothi

tea.note: Rooibos, red bush tea, is South Africa's own

water.note: Tap water is safe in most cities

hot.note: Literally "it is hot", of food, drinks, and the weather

cheers.note: Literally "life, health". Cheers! in English is just as common

bill.note: Tips of 10 to 15% are usual in restaurants

help.note: Shout it. The police are on 10111; from a mobile, 112

need-doctor.note: For an ambulance, call 10177, or 112 from a mobile

pharmacy.note: From chemist, the South African word for a pharmacy. Clicks and Dis-Chem are the big chains
